title: Title
notes: Open the lecture by framing spherical inference as an estimation problem on a curved sample space. The observations are unit vectors, so the arithmetic average is useful only after it is interpreted geometrically as a resultant vector with both direction and length.

title: Route
notes: Use this route slide to separate the chapter into decisions rather than formulas. The central theme is that each statistic has a target alternative, so exploratory plots and model assumptions determine which inferential tool is meaningful.

title: Spherical Sample
notes: Establish notation before discussing tests. The resultant direction is undefined if the resultant length is essentially zero, and that failure is not just numerical noise; it is evidence that the data may be uniform, girdle-like, or antipodal.

title: Exploratory Spherical Analysis
notes: For the reference notebook sample, the EDA numbers already suggest a tight cluster: n equals 64, Rbar is about 0.905, and the estimated cone is narrow. Stress that these summaries are prompts for modeling, not a substitute for inspecting the spherical pattern.

title: Fisher Model
notes: Introduce the Fisher density as the spherical analogue of a centered normal family, while avoiding the false impression that the sphere has Euclidean tails. The sufficient summaries are the resultant direction and length because the log likelihood depends on the sample through their dot product with mu.

title: Estimating Kappa
notes: Walk through kappa estimation as a one-dimensional inverse problem. The graph helps learners see why larger mean resultant length forces larger concentration, while also showing why the estimate should be interpreted only after the data actually look Fisher-like.

title: Confidence Cone
notes: Make the confidence cone concrete by translating it into a cap on the unit sphere. A listener should hear that the final report is angular: the direction is estimated by a pole, and uncertainty is the largest allowed angle from that pole.

title: Cap Probability
notes: Use the cap comparison to connect estimation with testing. The same angular region can be evaluated under two models, and the difference in mass explains why concentrated spherical samples quickly become incompatible with a uniform null.

title: Uniformity Tests
notes: Contrast first-moment and second-moment evidence. Rayleigh is powerful against a single mean shift, while Bingham-style tests are designed for departures that alter the orientation tensor without creating a large resultant vector. Ask students which point in the diagram each alternative would occupy before naming the test.

title: Alternative Geometry
notes: This taxonomy prevents a common mistake: treating any rejection of uniformity as evidence for a Fisher cluster. Axial and girdle alternatives can be very non-uniform while having nearly zero resultant, so the visualization determines the testing strategy.

title: Axial Diagnostics
notes: Explain that the scatter matrix is the right object when the observation is an axis rather than an arrow. Its eigenvalues reveal whether mass piles up near one axis, spreads around a great circle, or resembles uniform spherical noise.

title: Test Selection
notes: Turn the catalogue of tests into a routing problem. The instructor should ask what kind of departure would matter in the application, because the same data can be compelling under one lens and nearly invisible under another.

title: Simulation Calibration
notes: Use the simulation lab to make confidence coverage empirical. The three settings show the expected trend: more data and stronger concentration produce narrower cones, while finite-sample containment remains a quantity worth checking rather than assuming.

title: Notebook Artifacts
notes: Connect the lecture deck back to the computational notebook without turning the slide into a file inventory. The artifacts provide evidence for the claims: geometry for interpretation, simulation for calibration, and numerical checks for implementation trust.

title: Pitfalls
notes: Use the pitfalls slide as a quality-control checklist for student analyses. The main message is that spherical inference is not ordinary multivariate inference with spherical pictures added; the sample space changes the summaries, uncertainty sets, and diagnostics.

title: Recap
notes: Close by asking learners to identify which geometric feature a statistic is measuring before they compute it. The exercise is intentionally about a girdle-like eigenvalue pattern, where the mean resultant gives little evidence but the orientation tensor gives a clear clue.
